content: Data collection systems should focus on gathering information that is systematically useful for patient care and program management. Overloading these systems with unnecessary details, especially when electronic systems are introduced, should be avoided as it wastes resources and demotivates staff. In settings where routine monitoring and evaluation (M&E) capacity is still developing, ministries of health and national programs may consider periodic analyses of medical records using simple sampling methods. These reviews can also include investigations into medication adherence and drug safety. For example, annual patient record reviews can be conducted efficiently by program staff with minimal financial and training resources, focusing on household contacts. In many settings, data on people living with HIV (PLHIV) receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) are captured in electronic systems, enabling analyses using unique personal identifiers (UIDs). This allows for cohort analyses, such as tracking PLHIV newly enrolled in HIV care who were screened for tuberculosis (TB), evaluated for TB preventive treatment (TPT) eligibility, started on TPT, and completed TPT. UIDs help eliminate duplicate entries and improve data reliability for program management. Monitoring TPT completion is critical for both individual care and program management. Electronic data capture tools should record treatment outcomes for each individual starting TPT, including the minimum number of doses required for completion based on the regimen. National TB and HIV programs use various tools, such as patient cards, medical histories, case files, or electronic medical records, to document TPT services. However, scaling up TPT services faces challenges, including the need to capture diverse data often reliant on paper-based records and multiple healthcare providers. Programs monitoring TPT frequently use paper tools, such as household contact investigation lists or additional columns in antiretroviral (ARV) registers, to record TPT initiation among PLHIV. These tools are periodically reviewed to derive indicators, often requiring manual computation, which adds to the burden on healthcare workers. Increasingly, TB program data are being recorded electronically for individuals with TB disease requiring treatment, including ART. These databases generate M&E indicators and track patient treatment responses. However, many programs still lack systematic electronic data collection mechanisms for TPT activities. The World Health Organization (WHO) encourages the development of electronic systems to capture data elements needed for TPT care and monitoring, enabling automatic generation of indicators. For example, a review of medical records can assess TPT coverage and completion among household contacts of TB patients. This involves sampling health facilities treating TB patients, retrieving medical records of index patients (those with bacteriologically confirmed TB), and calculating key indicators such as the proportion of household contacts investigated for TB, eligible for TPT, initiated on TPT, and completed TPT. Missing data should be recorded and reported, and corrective actions should be taken if the proportion of missing data is high. WHO has developed a mobile application to support monitoring and evaluation of TPT, which is compatible with various electronic data systems. This app helps healthcare workers collect person-specific data and visualize them on an online dashboard for real-time monitoring. It can be adapted to meet country-specific program needs. As access to affordable hardware, software, and connectivity increases globally, real-time monitoring of TPT performance becomes more feasible. Countries should allocate dedicated budgets for digitizing data capture and reporting, and seek donor funding if necessary. Data confidentiality is paramount in providing optimal TPT and care. Personal information must be treated with the utmost confidentiality, shared only with those providing direct care, and securely stored. Computerized databases containing sensitive information should be protected with passwords and encryption, with access rights granted based on user roles. Assigning UIDs to individuals being evaluated for or receiving TPT can help match and de-duplicate entries. Personal details should be removed as soon as they are no longer required for reporting purposes. Supportive supervision is essential for routine M&E of health facilities, including quality checks for data recording and reporting. National programs may provide standard checklists to assess data quality and implementation across the TPT care cascade. Supervisory visits may also gather data for health management information system (HMIS) reporting. At least once a year, a data quality audit of routine monitoring systems should be conducted by the supervision team, involving members of both TB and HIV programs. Ethical considerations are critical in TPT implementation. Only 5–10% of individuals infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis will develop TB disease in their lifetime, but the risk is higher for certain groups, such as PLHIV, young children, and those recently infected. TPT should be administered after evaluating the benefits versus potential harms to the individual. Routine testing and treatment should be limited to groups with demonstrated risk of progression from TB infection to disease. TPT must always be an individual choice, made with full information and without coercion. Informed consent is generally required for TPT, as the subject does not pose an immediate risk to others, and the potential benefits are context-specific. Effective communication of possible uncertainties and risks is essential. Nurses and frontline healthcare workers can be trained to counsel individuals about TPT, interpret test results, and manage adverse events. National programs should develop culturally and linguistically appropriate TPT communication strategies, involving communities and individuals who have taken TPT. TPT is a proven intervention to prevent TB disease, reducing the risk by 60–90% compared to those who do not receive TPT. It is a critical component of the global strategy to end TB, particularly in low-incidence settings. Shorter rifamycin-based TPT regimens are more likely to be completed and are easier to manage programmatically, with greater potential to save lives. National programs should prioritize TPT for high-risk groups, such as household contacts of TB patients and PLHIV, and integrate TPT into active TB case-finding components. In conclusion, person-centered TPT care should be provided equitably, without placing marginalized populations at a disadvantage. Ministries of health should formulate appropriate TPT communication strategies and allocate resources to strengthen counseling efforts, enabling individuals to make informed choices about TPT.
